Part II — Statistics, Geometry and the Shape of an Image

What the codes Z and the dictionary D look like when one measures them, and what a single image looks like in activation space. The paper uses these observations to argue that a purely linear, near-orthogonal picture is incomplete.

After this page you can
  • read Figure 9 and explain the triangular envelope, the three dense positional concepts, and why a dense concept is awkward for a code with k=8 active entries;
  • decode the two baselines of Appendix E for the spectrum of Z⊤Z, and say why the evidence of Figure 9 (right) is weak;
  • compute the Welch bound, the typical coherence of random vectors, the tight-frame singular value c/d​ and the Marchenko–Pastur band, and use them to read Figure 10;
  • explain antipodal atoms with a non-negative code, and the cosine-similarity pitfall (Figure 11 A);
  • derive the trace identity tr[Z⊤ZDD⊤]=∥ZD∥F2​ and say what it does and does not imply for Figure 11 B;
  • explain how a PCA map is made, why PCA cannot create curvature, and what Figures 12, 13, 22 and 27 show;
  • define the position basis P, read Figures 14 and 15, and spot the inconsistency between stable rank and R2 in Figure 14;
  • state the "interpolative geometry" argument from the DINO/iBOT heads and KoLeo, and say which part is a conjecture.

Before you start#

Part II of the paper has no theorem. It measures things: how often and how strongly concepts fire, how the atoms sit relative to each other, and what the tokens of one image look like. The tone is descriptive; the conclusion ("beyond the LRH") is a reading of those measurements, and we mark where it goes further than they do.

How to read this page#

Each section starts with a one-line summary, quotes the paper in a paper box with the page of the arXiv v3 PDF, and decodes it. Every figure of the paper is shown and followed by a "How to read this figure" box. Remarks of ours are in Our reading boxes and are developed on page 6. Numbers that are not in the paper (marked "our estimate" or "recomputed") come from checks/check_04.py.

The story of the page in seven steps#

  1. Occurrence. Most concepts fire rarely; three concepts about position fire on about a quarter of all tokens (Fig. 9 A–C).
  2. Co-activation. The Gram matrix Z⊤Z has a smooth spectrum, between two baselines (Fig. 9 right).
  3. Geometry of the atoms. Inner products have heavy tails, singular values decay fast, atoms are distributed over many coordinates (Fig. 10).
  4. Antipodal pairs, and usage versus geometry. Some atoms are almost opposite; co-activation explains little of the geometry (Fig. 11).
  5. The shape of an image. PCA maps of the patch tokens of one image are smooth and follow objects (Figs. 12, 13, 22).
  6. Position. A position basis that is high-rank in early layers and two-dimensional in late ones; smoothness survives its removal (Figs. 14, 15, 27).
  7. Interpolative geometry. A conjecture that tokens are mixtures of prototypes; page 5 turns it into the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis.

What you need#

  • Coherence, Welch bound, Grassmannian frames, Johnson–Lindenstrauss, tight frames and the Marchenko–Pastur band: frames.
  • Stable rank, Hoyer score, cosine similarity: scores. PCA: PCA.
  • The dictionary D, codes Z, the archetypal SAE: dictionary learning. The tokens (cls, registers, patches): tokens.
  • The setup of page 3: LRH setup, token types.

Notation decoder#

SymbolMeaning hereSize
Atoken activations (rows = tokens); not the attention matrixnt×d
Zsparse non-negative codes, at most k=8 non-zeros per rownt×c
Ddictionary, one unit atom Di​ per row, A≈ZDc×d
G=Z⊤Zco-activation Gram matrix of the codes: Gij​=∑tokens​Z⋅i​Z⋅j​c×c
DD⊤Gram matrix of the atoms: inner products ⟨Di​,Dj​⟩c×c
Pposition basis: one vector per grid position, for one layer256×d
c,d,k,t32,000 atoms, 768 width, 8 active codes, 261 tokens per image

Two sizes need care. Z has one row per token, over all images: with 1.4M images that is about 3.65×108 rows (our estimate: 1.4×106×261). The matrix G is therefore a sum over more than 3×108 tokens, and the paper's "number of firings" counts tokens, not images.

1. How often and how strongly concepts fire#

For almost every concept, the rarer it is, the higher its energy when it fires (a triangular envelope in Fig. 9 A). Three concepts break the pattern: they fire on roughly a quarter of all tokens and encode position (left, right, bottom).

The problem#

The LRH says a token uses few concepts out of many. That is a statement about the support of the code. It says nothing about two other things one can measure directly on Z: how often each concept is on (its frequency), and how large it is when on (its energy). If the dictionary behaved like a pure sparse code, we would expect every concept to be rare. The paper looks for exceptions.

What the paper plots#

Concept occurrence statistics §5 · p. 11, Fig. 9 · p. 11

"[...] its conditional energy E(Zi​∣Zi​>0), the expected activation given that it fires, plotted against its firing count, i.e., the number of datapoints where Zi​ is nonzero. For the majority of concepts, the points are distributed within a triangular envelope [...]. [...] three outlier concepts that exhibit an anomalously dense activation pattern, firing across the entire dataset. [...] they encode positional information: specifically indicating whether a token lies on the left, right, or bottom of the input image grid. [...] we observe a hybrid representational regime where a small set of universally-active (here spatially grounded) features coexists with a broader ensemble of highly selective, image-contingent activations."

Zi​
the code of concept i on one token: a non-negative number, zero on most tokens.
E(Zi​∣Zi​>0)
conditional energy: the mean of Zi​ over the tokens where it is non-zero. It ignores the zeros, unlike E[Zi​] used for importance on page 3.
number of firings
the count of tokens (not images) with Zi​>0. Maximum: the number of tokens, about 3.65×108.
"energy"
the size of the code, hence of the contribution Zi​Di​ to a=zD (atoms have unit norm). The paper writes "norm regimes".
"dense"
active on a large fraction of tokens (reference: Sun et al. 2025, dense latents in SAEs).
How to read this figure
  • Axes. Horizontal: firing count (the bulk is below about 2×106, the outliers are near 0.95–1.15×108). Vertical: conditional energy, from 0 to about 5.
  • The bulk. A triangle: at low counts the energies are spread from small to large values; as the count grows, the largest energies disappear. Frequent concepts are weak when they fire.
  • The three outliers. Energy about 1.2–1.3, count about 108: far right, at a modest height. Panels B and C show them on example images: they light up a side of the image (left, right, bottom) regardless of the content.
  • What the authors conclude. Concepts live in different energy regimes, and the code is a hybrid: sparse selective concepts plus a few universal positional ones.
  • What the figure does not show. The shape of the triangle is not explained (no model, no axis scale given for the energy of the typical token); and it says nothing about which concepts sit in the bulk.

How dense is "dense"? A back-of-envelope estimate#

Our estimate — from the numbers of the paper

The paper trains on 1.4M ImageNet images (t=261 tokens each) and reads outlier counts of about 0.95 to 1.15×108 off the figure. The following uses these two readings; the exact counts are not in the text.

  1. Tokens: 1.4×106×261≈3.65×108.a row of Z per token.
  2. An outlier firing 0.95–1.15×108 times is active on 26% to 31% of all tokens.ratio of the count to the number of tokens.
  3. A typical concept fires fewer than 2×106 times, i.e. on less than 0.55% of the tokens.the same ratio, using the right edge of the bulk.
  4. Total activations: k×3.65×108≈2.9×109 (if every token uses exactly its k=8 slots).BatchTopK keeps k per token on average, so this is an average count.
  5. Three outliers at 1.05×108 each take 3.15×108 activations: about 11% of all activations (range 10–12%).3.15×108/2.9×109.
  6. The mean concept fires 2.9×109/32,000≈9×104 times, so the three outliers fire about 1000 times more often than the average one.1.05×108/9.1×104≈1150.
Why an always-on feature is awkward for a sparse code

A code with k=8 active entries per token has a budget of 8 slots per token. A concept that is on in 29% of the tokens occupies one of those slots in 29% of the tokens; three such concepts occupy 3×0.287≈0.86 slots per token on average (our estimate; the three are probably not independent, since "left" and "right" cannot hold at once). So about one slot in nine is not spent on image content but on position. More basically, a feature that is almost always on carries little information per token about the token: it behaves like a bias or a slowly varying coordinate, which is what a dense low-rank component is. The paper's analogy is "sparse plus dense low-rank" representations.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: start with 0 dense concepts: all dots in the triangle. Add three and move their frequency: the number of slots they take per token and their share of all activations follow the arithmetic above. Increase k: the same dense concepts take a smaller share. The cloud is a toy (our generator, not the paper's data); only the arithmetic of the readout is general.

What the paper links to

The text connects the three outliers to two other results: positional information is linearly decodable up to intermediate layers (section 8, Fig. 14) and forms a 2-dimensional subspace at the penultimate layer. A 2-D position subspace fits with three dense concepts: "left" and "right" are two opposite ends of the horizontal coordinate and "bottom" is one end of the vertical one (see the antipodal section for why one signed coordinate needs two non-negative atoms).

Our reading — "dense" is a threshold, and the triangle is not explained

The paper does not give a definition of dense, nor the exact counts. The triangle is plausible from a norm budget (tokens have a roughly bounded norm, so a concept cannot be both frequent and large), but this is our intuition, not a result. Also, the measured quantity is per token over all token types: it does not say whether the three concepts fire on registers and cls. See page 6.

A concept fires on 0.3% of the tokens with mean code 3. Another fires on 30% with mean code 1.2. Which has the larger E[Zi​], and which the larger conditional energy?

Answer

E[Z]=frequency×conditional energy: 0.003×3=0.009 against 0.3×1.2=0.36. The dense one has 40 times the mean code, the rare one a 2.5 times larger conditional energy. That is why the paper plots conditional energy against the count: E[Z] would mix the two.

Reflex

When you see "mean activation" of a sparse code → ask whether zeros are included. E[Zi​] includes them, E[Zi​∣Zi​>0] does not.

2. Co-activation: the Gram matrix of the codes#

The matrix G=Z⊤Z counts, for each pair of concepts, how strongly they fire together. Its spectrum decays smoothly: no gap, no dominant mode. The paper reads this as "no block structure"; against its two baselines the evidence is weak.

The problem#

If concepts came in modules (all "dog" concepts together, all "texture" concepts together), tokens would use whole modules at once and the co-activation matrix would be block-diagonal, with a few large eigenvalues (one per module) and a gap after them. The question is whether G looks like that.

Concepts co-occurrence §5 · p. 11–12, Fig. 9 right · p. 11

"The Gram matrix of concept co-activation G=Z⊤Z∈Rc×c [...] has a spectrum that decays smoothly, with no gaps or dominant modes, providing little evidence for modular low-rank structure. As reference points, we create two baselines, one from random activations Z with same sparsity (random), and one directly shuffling the coactivation matrix G (shuffle). Relative to baselines, it lies between the steep decay of the random surrogate and the inflated tail of the shuffled one. Below both would imply redundancy, above both extreme diffuseness; its intermediate position instead reflects a high-dimensional, distributed regime where concepts co-activate without forming clear clusters."

What G is and what its spectrum can show#

  1. Gij​=∑n​Zn,i​Zn,j​ entry of Z⊤Z: sum over tokens n of the product of the codes of i and j. Non-zero only for tokens where both are on.
  2. Gii​=∑n​Zn,i2​ diagonal: total squared energy of concept i. Frequent and strong concepts have large diagonals.
  3. G⪰0, so its eigenvalues are ≥0 and ∑i​λi​=trG=∑i​Gii​ G=Z⊤Z is a Gram matrix; the trace is the sum of eigenvalues.
  4. If the concepts form m disjoint modules that never co-fire across modules, G is block-diagonal with m blocks, so its eigenvalues are the union of those of the blocks block-diagonal matrices decompose; a module whose members co-fire a lot gives one large eigenvalue.

So block structure shows up as a few large eigenvalues followed by a drop. A smooth decay with no drop means no such separation. Note what this cannot tell: dense positional concepts (section 1) have huge diagonal entries and co-fire with everything, which tends to create a few large eigenvalues; the paper does not discuss this.

The two baselines of Appendix E, formula by formula#

Baselines for the co-activation spectrum App. E · p. 37

Random baseline: Rij​=Uij​⋅1(Vij​<ρ) with Uij​,Vij​∼U(0,1), then R~=​R+R⊤​F​(R+R⊤)/2​⋅​Z⊤Z​F​, with diag(R~)=diag(Z⊤Z). Shuffled baseline: take the upper-triangular entries {Gij​:i<j}, permute them randomly, and put them back symmetrically, keeping the diagonal of G.

ρ
the density of G (fraction of non-zero entries); the paper says "identical sparsity ρ" without a formula.
Uij​, Vij​
U draws the value, V decides whether the entry exists: each entry is non-zero with probability ρ and then uniform in (0,1). Independent over pairs: no pair is special.
(R+R⊤)/2
symmetrisation, so that eigenvalues are real.
⋅ ​Z⊤Z​F​/​R+R⊤​F​
rescaling so that the total mass (Frobenius norm) matches. Since ​(R+R⊤)/2​F​=21​​R+R⊤​F​, the formula as written gives a Frobenius norm of 21​∥G∥F​ (checked in check_04.py); a global factor changes nothing on a normalised spectrum, so this is only a typo-level remark.
shuffle
keeps three things: the diagonal, the multiset of off-diagonal values, symmetry. Destroys: which pair gets which value.
What each baseline is a null for
  • Random: "same density and same total mass, but co-occurrences without any structure". Its spectrum has no outstanding modes.
  • Shuffled: "same values, scrambled pairs". Because ∑i​λi2​=∥G∥F2​ and ∑i​λi​=trG are the same for G and for the shuffle, the two spectra share total mass and total squared mass. If the original has structure, its energy is concentrated in fewer eigenvalues, so the shuffle (spread out) has the heavier tail. On a toy with 20 planted blocks (our simulation, check_04.py) the tenth eigenvalue is 0.59 of the first for G and 0.31 for its shuffle: structure gives a slower head and a lighter tail, which is the picture the paper describes.
How to read this figure
  • Axes. Horizontal: eigenvalue rank, 1 to 500. Vertical: normalised eigenvalue, log scale.
  • What to look at. No cliff in the original curve; it lies between the random curve (steeper) and the shuffled one (heavier tail).
  • Numbers. The three curves stay within a factor of about 1.3 of each other over the plotted range (our reading of the figure).
  • The authors' conclusion. Smooth and intermediate: co-activation is high-dimensional and distributed, without modules.
  • What it does not show. A test of the module hypothesis; only that the spectrum is not extreme in either direction.
Our reading — a factor 1.3 on a log axis is a weak signal

A log-scale plot makes small gaps look like gaps. The three curves differ by a factor of about 1.3, and no variability across random draws or subsamples is shown. "Between two baselines" is also what any matrix with partial structure would do. A better test is a statistic with a null distribution (for instance the top-eigenvalue share against many shuffles). See page 6.

Reflex

When you see "the spectrum lies between two baselines" → ask what each baseline preserves, and by how much the curves differ on a linear scale.

3. Geometry of the dictionary#

The 32,000 atoms are not spread like random vectors and not like a Grassmannian frame: inner products have heavy tails (up to about 0.9), singular values decay fast (the dictionary is anisotropic), and atoms are spread over many coordinates (Hoyer score about 0.22–0.25).

The problem and the reference points#

The LRH (Definition 1, page 3) asks for unit atoms with small coherence. "Small" needs a scale. The paper builds two reference dictionaries with the same c=32,000 and d=768.

Baselines for concept geometry App. F · p. 38

"Random vectors on sphere: we sample a Gaussian random matrix H∈Rc×d, Hij​∼N(0,1) i.i.d., and then we normalized each row to have L2 norm 1. [...] Grassmannian frame: [...] we numerically computed the Grassmannian frame of c atoms in d dimension. [...] we adapted the algorithm from recent work TAAP, [...] adapted it to CUDA [...] solving the frame once still takes 6hr on an A100 GPU. In the end, we reached maximal coherence of 0.065897."

Reminder — coherence, Welch bound, Grassmannian frames

Coherence of unit vectors: μ(D)=maxi=j​∣⟨Di​,Dj​⟩∣. For c>d unit vectors in Rd, the Welch bound says μ≥d(c−1)c−d​​; a Grassmannian frame is a set of c unit vectors minimising μ (it reaches the bound only for special (c,d)). more

Recomputed — the numbers behind the baselines
  1. Welch bound for c=32,000, d=768: (32000−768)/(768×31999)​≈0.0356. plug in; no frame can be below this.
  2. The computed Grassmannian frame has μ=0.0659: 1.85 times the Welch bound. 0.065897/0.03565. The bound is not tight for these sizes, so the numerical frame is only an approximation of the optimum (as the paper says).
  3. Random unit vectors: an inner product is approximately N(0,1/d), standard deviation 1/768​=0.0361. the inner product of two independent uniform points on the sphere has variance 1/d.
  4. There are c(c−1)/2≈5.1×108 pairs. The largest of P approximately Gaussian values is about 2lnP/d​=0.229. Gaussian tail: Pe−dμ2/2≈1. Matches the paper's "random within ±0.2" (a sample of 4000 atoms gives 0.196 in check_04.py).

Figure 10#

Geometry of concept vectors §5 · p. 12, Fig. 10 · p. 12

"(A) [...] the SAE dictionary exhibits heavier tails and a flatter central peak—indicative of higher coherence. [...] (B) SAE exhibits sharper decay than both baselines, suggesting lower effective rank and anisotropy: some directions are densely populated while others are sparse or unused. (C & D) [...] Scores remain below the neuron-aligned limit (1.0), indicating that concepts are not axis-aligned. Compared to baseline expectations (e.g., 1−2/π​≈0.202 for Gaussian vectors), the SAE atoms are slightly sparser, still supporting the notion of distributed representations."

How to read this figure
  • (A) Axes. Horizontal: ⟨Di​,Dj​⟩; vertical: log density. Ranges read off: random within about ±0.2, Grassmannian within about ±0.066, SAE from about −0.85 to +0.92, with the positive tail heavier.
  • (A) Reading. Most SAE pairs are weakly correlated, but a non-negligible fraction are strongly aligned: "tight clusters". The dictionary moves away from incoherence, not towards it.
  • (B) Axes. Index of the singular value against its value. SAE: about 22.5 at the start, about 7 at index 200, about 3.5 at index 760, near 0 at the very end. Random: from 7.4 to 5.5. Grassmannian: flat at about 6.5.
  • (C) Hoyer score of each atom: about 0.22–0.25 (one-hot =1, Gaussian ≈0.2). (D) UMAP of the atoms, coloured by that score.
  • Does not show. How many pairs lie in the tail (a log density hides counts), nor which atoms form the clusters.

(B) Singular values: tight frame, Marchenko–Pastur, anisotropy#

Reminder — tight frames and the spectrum of random matrices

D∈Rc×d with unit rows has ∑i≤d​σi2​=∥D∥F2​=c. If all singular values are equal, σi​=c/d​ and the rows form a tight frame (D⊤D=dc​I). For a random matrix with i.i.d. rows, the singular values fall in the Marchenko–Pastur band c/d​(1±d/c​). more

  1. Tight-frame level: c/d​=32000/768​=6.455. ∑σ2=c spread evenly over d values.
  2. Marchenko–Pastur band: 6.455×[1−0.155,1+0.155]=[5.45,7.45]. d/c​=0.155. A simulated random 32000×768 dictionary gives [5.47,7.45], matching the figure's "7.4→5.5".
  3. The Grassmannian frame is (almost) tight: flat at ≈6.5. minimal coherence goes with a nearly flat spectrum.
  4. The SAE: σ1​≈22.5, so σ12​≈506, i.e. 12 times the average c/d=41.7 and 1.6% of the total mass in one direction. 22.52/41.7=12.2 and 506/32000=1.6%.
Anisotropy

A set of atoms is anisotropic when their mass is not spread evenly over directions: some directions of Rd carry much more squared mass σ2 than others. Isotropic means all σi2​ equal to c/d. Here: a few directions hold much more mass, and the tail of singular values goes to almost 0, i.e. some directions of the space are practically unused by the dictionary.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: at 0 the atoms are uniform on the sphere and the singular values fill the Marchenko–Pastur band. Raise anisotropy: the first singular values grow above the band and the last fall below it, while ∑σ2 stays equal to c. Both are small-size versions (c=160, d=32) of the 32000×768 case.

Global anisotropy: two tentative explanations §5 · p. 12 and footnote

"One potential explanation is that the activations A themselves have anisotropic covariance, thus to reconstruct them A≈ZD with L2 error, more atoms are allocated to the more important and higher variance subspace." Footnote: "A speculative hypothesis is that the affine components of the last LayerNorm deforms the activation space into an ellipsoidal geometry, locally increasing curvature along some directions. In such regions, dictionary learning may require more atoms to adequately cover the manifold with low reconstruction error. While this remains to be formalized [...]"

  • First explanation. The atoms are in conv(A) (archetypal SAE) and the loss is ∥A−ZD∥F2​; high-variance directions of A matter more for the loss, so more atoms point there. This is checkable (compare the spectrum of D with the covariance spectrum of A); the paper does not do it.
  • Second explanation. After the last LayerNorm, LN(x)=γ⊙u+β with u centred and scaled to norm d​. If the entries of γ are non-zero, the output lies on an ellipsoid. The paper calls this speculative and unformalised.
Our reading — the two explanations are not exclusive, and the second is a real constraint

Both can hold: the ellipsoid shape is itself a source of anisotropic covariance. We test the ellipsoid claim in our experiments (page 6); it also bears on the Minkowski hypothesis of page 5.

(C–D) Hoyer scores: atoms are distributed#

Reminder — Hoyer sparsity

For x∈Rn, Hoyer(x)=n​−1n​−∥x∥1​/∥x∥2​​∈[0,1]: 1 for a one-hot vector, 0 for a constant one. more

For a Gaussian vector, ∥x∥1​/∥x∥2​≈2n/π​, so the score tends to 1−2/π​=0.202 (simulation at n=768: 0.210). An atom aligned with one neuron would score near 1; a vector with 77 equal non-zero entries (10% of 768) scores 0.71. The SAE atoms score 0.22–0.25: almost as spread as random vectors, slightly sparser. So each atom is a combination of many of the 768 coordinates: a distributed representation, not neuron-aligned.

Our reading — Hoyer depends on the basis

The score is measured in the coordinate basis of the residual stream, which the model has no reason to privilege except through LayerNorm's per-coordinate γ,β (and known high-norm coordinates in some ViTs). A score close to that of Gaussian vectors says the atoms are not axis-aligned; it does not say they are "as random as" Gaussian ones (they are not, by panels A and B).

Johnson–Lindenstrauss footnote §5 · p. 12

"The Johnson–Lindenstrauss (JL) lemma implies that p=exp(O(mε2)) vectors can be embedded into Rm such that all pairwise inner products are preserved up to a small distortion ε>0. This supports the feasibility of near-orthogonality even in regimes where p≫m."

Decoded: with m=d=768 dimensions one can place exponentially many (exp(O(768ε2))) unit vectors with all ∣⟨⋅,⋅⟩∣≤ε. Equivalently d≳ε−2lnc: with lnc=10.4, near-orthogonality at the 0.2 level needs a few hundred dimensions. So the LRH's "overcomplete but quasi-orthogonal" is feasible, and the paper's point is that the learned dictionary does not use this freedom (it prefers "structured redundancy"). more

What the paper concludes, and what to keep

The paper: the dictionary is "neither maximally incoherent nor uniformly distributed", with clusters, reduced effective rank, and groups of atoms tied to tasks (page 3). Keep apart: (A) is a statement about pairs (some are far above 0.066); (B) about the global spectrum; (C–D) about coordinates. None of them alone contradicts the LRH, since the LRH (Def. 1) only asks for small coherence ε to be some number; the paper's argument is that μ≈0.9 is not small.

Why must the singular values of a unit-row dictionary with c=32000, d=768 have mean square 41.7, whatever its geometry?

Answer

∑i=1d​σi2​=∥D∥F2​=∑j​∥Dj​∥2=c since rows are unit. Divide by d: c/d=41.7. A larger first singular value must be paid by smaller ones.

Reflex

When you see "the singular values decay" for a dictionary → compare with c/d​ and the Marchenko–Pastur band, not with a flat line at 1.

4. Antipodal pairs#

Some pairs of atoms satisfy Di​≈−Dj​: "vertical" against "horizontal" lines, white against black shirts, a person on the left against on the right. With non-negative codes, this is what a signed feature looks like.

The observation#

Antipodal structure §5 · p. 12, Fig. 11 A · p. 13

"[...] a small but significant number of concept pairs are nearly antipodal, i.e., Di​≈−Dj​. This go against the assumption of a Grassmannian-like dictionary. Instead, it suggests that DINO sometimes exploits paired directions to encode semantically opposed features such as 'left vs right' or 'white vs black' along shared lines but with opposite signs. Practically, such antipodal structure should be accounted when using cosine similarity in downstream analyses, particularly in data filtering, clustering, or retrieval contexts."

How to read this figure
  • What is drawn. Each row is a pair (i,j) with ⟨Di​,Dj​⟩≈−1; for each concept, example images where it is strongly active.
  • What to look at. The two concepts of a pair are semantic opposites (vertical/horizontal, white/black, left/right).
  • The authors' conclusion. Polarity encodes meaning: the model uses one line with two signs.
  • What it does not show. How many pairs there are ("a small but significant number"), nor a control with unpaired concepts. These are the examples found at the tail of Fig. 10 A.

Why non-negative codes need two atoms for one signed feature#

Worked example — one axis, one signed feature

Suppose a token carries a feature x∈R along a unit direction u: the activation is a=xu, with x=−1.5, 0.7 or 2.

  1. With one atom D1​=u and codes z1​≥0: a=z1​u can only represent x≥0. For x=−1.5, the best code is z1​=0 and the error is 1.5. a non-negative combination of one vector is a half-line.
  2. With two atoms D1​=u, D2​=−u: x=−1.5 is z=(0,1.5); x=0.7 is z=(0.7,0); x=2 is z=(2,0). z1​=max(x,0), z2​=max(−x,0), so that z1​D1​+z2​D2​=(z1​−z2​)u=xu.
  3. Cosine similarity of the two atoms: −1. Coherence ∣⟨D1​,D2​⟩∣=1, the largest possible. they span one line.
  4. The two codes never need to be on together: z1​z2​=0 in the representation above. So their entry G12​ of the co-activation matrix is about 0. simultaneous activity would give (z1​−z2​)u, a waste of one of the k slots; our reasoning, not a statement of the paper.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: with the second atom at 180∘, the error is 0 for every x. Reduce the angle: negative x can no longer be reached and the error grows. The line through the origin needs two opposite directions, not one.

Reminder — cosine similarity

cos(x,y)=⟨x,y⟩/(∥x∥∥y∥)∈[−1,1]. It sees the direction, with sign. more

The cosine pitfall

Two antipodal concepts have cosine −1: a nearest-neighbour search or a clustering by cosine puts them as far apart as possible, although they are the same axis seen from its two ends (the same line, the same feature). Conversely, a filter "remove concepts with large ∣cos∣ with a given one" removes the opposite too, while one that keeps only cosines >0 misses it. Decide first whether the sign is meaning (left versus right) or redundancy (one line), then use cos or ∣cos∣.

Our reading — antipodal pairs may come from non-negativity, not from the model

The paper opposes the pairs to the Grassmannian assumption. But the codes are constrained to Z≥0: an unconstrained signed feature (the usual LRH) would be one atom. The pairs may thus be a consequence of the dictionary method (non-negative codes) applied to signed directions, in addition to whatever the model does. The paper's evidence cannot separate the two. It also means that the coherence μ, which uses ∣⟨Di​,Dj​⟩∣, equals 1 for such a pair although the representation is perfectly legitimate. See page 6.

5. Geometry versus usage#

Fig. 11 B: the co-activation matrix Z⊤Z and the geometry matrix DD⊤ have correlation r=0.28 (R2=0.08). Atoms that fire together are only slightly closer. A footnote adds that a positive correlation is expected from the reconstruction itself.

Concept geometry is only weakly shaped by co-activation §5 · p. 13, Fig. 11 B · p. 13

"A natural hypothesis [...] is that the geometry of the concept dictionary reflects patterns of co-activation [...]. To evaluate this, we compare the co-activation matrix Z⊤Z [...] with the geometric affinity matrix DD⊤. [...] the two matrices exhibit only weak but statistically significant correlation. [...] Footnote: Algebraically, [...] corr(Z⊤Z,DD⊤)∝tr[Z⊤ZDD⊤]=tr[D⊤Z⊤ZD]≈tr[A⊤A]∝cov(A), which is guaranteed to be positive. So this positive relation might be an intrinsic property of linear reconstructive methods." Right panel: a UMAP of the dictionary with the top co-activation links drawn.

How to read this figure
  • Left. Each point is a pair of concepts: horizontal, ⟨Di​,Dj​⟩ (geometry); vertical, Gij​ (usage). A weak upward trend inside a wide cloud: r=0.28, R2=r2≈0.08 (0.282=0.078).
  • Right. If co-firing concepts were neighbours in the UMAP, edges would be short and local. They are long and tangled: co-activation links cross the map.
  • Conclusion of the authors. Usage statistics do not determine proximity; there is no clear modular organisation.
  • What it does not say. Whether the diagonal is in the correlation, how many pairs, and whether the Pearson correlation was computed on raw or log values.

The footnote's trace identity, step by step#

Row convention: Z∈RN×c (N tokens), D∈Rc×d, G=Z⊤Z, K=DD⊤ (both c×c and symmetric).

  1. ⟨G,K⟩F​=∑ij​Gij​Kij​=tr[G⊤K]=tr[GK] the entrywise inner product of two matrices is tr[G⊤K]; G is symmetric.
  2. tr[Z⊤ZDD⊤]=tr[D⊤Z⊤ZD] cyclic property of the trace, tr[XY]=tr[YX], applied with X=Z⊤ZD and Y=D⊤: the last factor D⊤ moves to the front.
  3. tr[(ZD)⊤(ZD)]=∥ZD∥F2​ D⊤Z⊤=(ZD)⊤, and tr[M⊤M]=∑ij​Mij2​.
  4. ∥ZD∥F2​≈∥A∥F2​ ZD≈A with R2>88%.

Verified numerically on random 50×12 codes and a 12×7 dictionary: all four expressions equal 1428.37 (check_04.py).

Our reading — what the identity gives, and what it does not

The identity is exact and the quantity ⟨G,K⟩F​=∥ZD∥F2​ is positive: it is the uncentred inner product of the two matrices. Hence "any linear reconstruction gives a positive relation" is true for this inner product. But a Pearson correlation centres both matrices, is not proportional to this trace ("∝" in the footnote is loose), and does not need the diagonal. Two points follow.

  • The diagonal terms dominate the trace: Gii​>0 and Kii​=1. In a toy with 300 unit atoms and unrelated sparse codes (check_04.py), 99.8% of ⟨G,K⟩F​ comes from the diagonal and the Pearson correlation on the off-diagonal entries is 0.002, while including the diagonal gives 0.40.
  • So if the paper's r=0.28 includes the diagonal it is of the size that unrelated usage and geometry give; if it excludes it, then it is a small but real relation. The paper does not say which (the figure does not tell either).

Either way, r=0.28 is weak evidence that usage does not shape geometry. See page 6.

r=0.28, so R2=0.08. What percentage of the variance of Gij​ does geometry "explain" in the linear sense?

Answer

r2=0.078, about 8% (as read off the paper): for a simple linear regression of one variable on the other, R2=r2.

6. What the LRH predicts and what the paper observes#

One table: for each prediction of the linear representation hypothesis (Definition 1), what §5 observes and where. The last column is our reading of how strong the evidence is.

The LRH predictsThe paper observesWhereEvidence (ours)
Sparse codes: concepts rarely active (at most k≪c per token)Three dense positional concepts, each on about 26–31% of tokens (our estimate); hybrid sparse + denseFig. 9 A–Csolid (a count)
Quasi-orthogonal atoms, coherence ≤ε small (Grassmannian is possible: 0.066)Heavy tails, inner products from about −0.85 to +0.92Fig. 10 Asolid (but see antipodal)
No preferred directions: atoms spread evenly (tight frame, σi​≈c/d​=6.5)Fast singular value decay, σ1​≈22.5, tail near 0Fig. 10 Bsolid; the explanation is speculative
Atoms are arbitrary distributed directions (not neuron-aligned)Hoyer ≈0.22–0.25: distributedFig. 10 C–Dconsistent with the LRH, not against it
A signed feature is one direction (one atom)Antipodal pairs Di​≈−Dj​Fig. 11 Asuggestive (non-negative codes explain it)
Geometry is a free parameter; usage statistics are not part of the modelWeak link between Z⊤Z and DD⊤ (r=0.28); smooth, gap-free spectrum of Z⊤ZFig. 9 right, Fig. 11 Bsuggestive (weak, see footnote identity)
Says nothing on the set of tokens of an imagePer-image PCA maps are smooth, follow objects, share a global frameFigs. 12, 13, 22suggestive (qualitative)
Position is one more concept among manyPosition basis high rank early, 2-D plane late; smoothness survives its removalFigs. 14, 15, 27suggestive (with an inconsistency, section 8)
What the paper does and does not say

The paper writes that these patterns "are difficult to reconcile with a purely linear superposition model, and instead point toward additional geometric constraints" (§5 · p. 14). Its own limitations section (App. J · p. 51) says it refrains from stating that the results contradict the LRH. Each row above is compatible with a generalised linear model (non-negative codes, anisotropic covariance); the paper's step from the table to the MRH is the subject of page 5.

7. The shape of an image: PCA maps#

The paper stops looking at the dictionary and looks at the 256 patch tokens of one image. Coloured by their first three principal components, they give smooth maps that follow objects. Since PCA is linear, the paper says it "cannot fabricate curvature"; this is true, but needs a precise statement.

The problem#

All of Part I and §5 went through a dictionary factorisation A≈ZD. §6 asks what the tokens look like without it ("model-native geometry"), in the simplest setting: the tokens of one image. The tool is the PCA map that Oquab et al. (DINOv2) and Darcet et al. (registers) already show to illustrate semantic structure.

The shape of an image §6 · p. 15

"[...] (i) to demystify what PCA actually captures in single-image embeddings, particularly the origin of the observed 'smooth' structure; and (ii) to characterize token-level geometry across layers without presupposing a sparse, near-orthogonal coding model." Captions of Figs. 12 and 13: "Patch embeddings from DINO are projected via PCA (on a per-image basis) and visualized by assigning the first three principal components to RGB color (normalized to [0,1]). [...] PCA is an affine (linear) transformation and cannot generate curvature on its own, implying that the observed smoothness reflects genuine structure in the embeddings." "[...] the alignment of token geometry across distinct images suggest that the representation is not purely relative (i.e., based only on distances within each image tokens)."

How a PCA map is made#

Reminder — PCA

For a data matrix X∈Rn×d, centre the rows, take the eigenvectors of the covariance (equivalently the right singular vectors) as principal directions v1​,v2​,… ordered by variance. The coordinate of row x on component r is ⟨x−xˉ,vr​⟩. more

  1. Take the 256 patch tokens of one image: X∈R256×768. the paper's maps use patch tokens; cls and registers are left out.
  2. Centre them and compute the top three principal directions of this image's tokens. "per-image basis": one PCA per image.
  3. Project: each token gets three numbers (u1​,u2​,u3​). 256×3 matrix.
  4. Rescale each of the three channels to [0,1] and read them as (r,g,b). the caption says "normalized to [0,1]"; whether per channel or jointly is not stated.
  5. Put the 256 colours back on the 16×16 grid of patches. token (i,j) keeps its position; the map is an image.
Signs and colours are only meaningful inside one image

A principal direction is defined up to sign, and its rank depends on the image. The colour "red" in two different per-image maps does not mean the same thing. That is why Fig. 22 (below) uses one shared basis.

"PCA is linear, so it cannot fabricate curvature", made precise#

Fact

Let L:Rd→R3 be affine, L(x)=Px+b. For two points a,b′, the image of the segment [a,b′] is the segment [La,Lb′], or a single point when La=Lb′.

  1. A point of the segment is xt​=(1−t)a+tb′, t∈[0,1]. definition of the segment.
  2. L(xt​)=P((1−t)a+tb′)+b=(1−t)(Pa+b)+t(Pb′+b)=(1−t)La+tLb′. linearity of P, and (1−t)b+tb=b.
  3. So t↦L(xt​) is the parametrisation of the segment from La to Lb′; if the two endpoints coincide, a single point. □ same formula as the segment.

Consequence: if the colours of the PCA map trace a curved surface, that curvature was already present in the projection of the data onto the three directions. A projection can lose shape (flatten, as in the right panel), never add curvature to a straight set. This is the correct content of the paper's sentence.

Our reading — what a smooth map does and does not prove

A projection onto orthonormal directions can only shrink distances: ∥Px−Py∥≤∥x−y∥. So if neighbouring patches are close in R768, they are close in colour. The converse fails: two tokens can have the same colour and differ in all the other 765 directions. A smooth map therefore shows that the top-3 coordinates vary slowly across the image; it is consistent with, but does not prove, that the tokens form a connected set in R768. Moreover, neighbouring patches of a natural image look alike, so some smoothness is expected from the content; the paper does not give a null comparison (for example, the same maps for pixel patches). See page 6.

"Locally connected"

The paper uses "locally connected" and "smooth" without defining them. The operational meaning in the figures: tokens of adjacent patches are neighbours in the embedding, so that the 256 tokens trace a connected low-dimensional set (a curve or a sheet) rather than a cloud, and colour boundaries follow object boundaries.

Figures 12, 13, 22#

How to read Figures 12 and 13
  • What is drawn. A photo and, next to it, a 16×16 map of colours (RGB = the first three per-image principal components).
  • What to look at. Regions of nearly constant colour with sharp edges at object contours; the object and its background get different colours; a few noisy patches remain.
  • Authors' conclusion. Despite no supervision for localisation, tokens lie on smooth low-dimensional manifolds aligned with objects (and PCA cannot create this).
  • Does not show. Any quantitative measure of smoothness; the selection of images (Fig. 12 says random, Fig. 13 is a single class); a comparison with another model.
How to read this figure
  • Difference with Figs. 12–13. One PCA is fitted on the tokens of all five images pooled together (5×256 tokens), then every image is projected in that same basis.
  • Columns. Photo; colour map (the leopard is red in all five, the top is green, the sides blue, the bottom dark); then five views of the 3D token cloud, coloured by RGB.
  • What to look at. The five clouds have the same branched shape in the same place: the red cluster of the animal, a green and a blue branch.
  • Authors' conclusion. "A global manifold structure, within which local image tokenizations trace smooth trajectories": the representation is not purely relative.
  • Does not show. Images of different classes or layouts; five similar images (one animal, centred, in a forest) are favourable for alignment.
Why a shared basis shows the geometry is "not purely relative"

A purely relative representation would be one in which only the distances between tokens of the same image are meaningful; then the position of the clouds in the ambient space of different images would be arbitrary, and a PCA basis pooled over images would not align them. Here the clouds overlap and the colours agree. It is a statement about these five images, not a proof for arbitrary ones.

A linear map sends a straight line of tokens (two tokens and all their convex combinations) to a curve in the PCA map. Is that possible?

Answer

No: the image of a segment under a linear (or affine) map is a segment or a point. A curved trace in a PCA map means the tokens themselves do not lie on a straight line; it says nothing about the original curvature in the discarded directions.

8. Position: is the smoothness just position?#

A position basis P (one vector per grid position, per layer) is high-rank in early layers and collapses to about two dimensions in the last ones. In per-image PCA it shows up only in components 3 to 5, and the maps stay smooth when the position subspace is projected out.

The problem#

The ViT adds position information at the input and every patch token is tied to a place in the grid. A smooth colour map over a grid could simply be that: tokens that are neighbours in the image have similar position codes. The paper tests this ("Just position?") in three steps: build a position basis, see how it changes with depth, check whether it explains the PCA maps.

The position basis P and its two extractions#

Positional basis extraction App. I · p. 45; §6 · p. 15

"For each layer, we extract positional embeddings from 1 million ImageNet images, yielding A∈RN×t×d token representations [...]. We employ two approaches to recover the positional basis: Direct averaging. We compute the average embedding for each spatial position across all images: pi​=N1​∑k=1N​An,i​ [...]. Linear classification. We train a linear classifier to predict token position from embeddings, yielding weight vectors wi​ for each position at each layer. Both methods produce highly consistent results [...]. We therefore choose to use the classifier weights as our primary positional basis." Main text: "a position encoding matrix P∈R256×d at each layer".

P∈R256×d
row i is the vector for grid position i of the 16×16 grid, at a given layer. 256 rows because only the patch tokens have a grid position.
direct averaging
pi​ is the mean activation of the token at position i over images: whatever is constant across images at this position (content averages out). The paper writes An,i​ with a sum over k — an index slip: it should read N1​∑n=1N​An,i​.
linear classification
a 256-way linear classifier i^=argmaxi​⟨a,wi​⟩ (+bias, not mentioned). Its weight rows wi​ are the basis: a direction along which position i is read out. Accuracy = fraction of tokens whose position is recovered.
Notation in the paper

The appendix uses N and n for the number of images and t=261 for tokens per image; only the 256 patch tokens have a position. We write N for the number of images.

Figure 14: decoding, rank, per-image PCA#

How to read Fig. 14 (top left)
  • Axes. Horizontal: layer 0 to 11. Vertical: accuracy of the position decoder.
  • Numbers (read off). About 1.0 in layers 0–2, 0.97 in layers 3–4, 0.95 in layer 5, 0.92 in layers 6–7, 0.82 in layer 8, then 0.44, 0.34, 0.23 in layers 9, 10, 11. The curves for cls and registers stay high until the end.
  • Reading. Exact position is recoverable up to layer 8, then lost; the caption says "collapses after layer 8".
  • Not shown. The chance level (1/256=0.004) and the structure of the errors: at layers 9–11, a decoder that is off by one patch is counted as wrong; so a coarse position can still be present (see Fig. 15).
Reminder — stable rank

For a matrix with singular values σ1​≥σ2​≥…, srank(P)=∥P∥F2​/∥P∥22​=∑r​σr2​/σ12​. It is 1 for a rank-one matrix, at most rankP, and it counts "how many directions are as strong as the strongest". more

How to read Fig. 14 (top right)
  • Left panel. Stable rank for layers 1 to 12: 9.0, 8.1, 5.4, 7.2, 5.6, 5.4, 4.9, 4.4, 4.4, 2.8, 2.6, 2.7; a dashed line at 2.
  • Right panel. R2 of the top two principal components of the position basis, for layers 0 to 11: 0.63, 0.75, 0.83, 0.77, 0.81, 0.86, 0.90, 0.94, 0.96, 0.99, 1.00, 1.00.
  • Reading. Early layers: many directions are needed to describe the 256 positions; late layers: two components describe 99–100% of the variance: a 2-D sheet.
  • Not shown. Whether P is centred before the stable rank; which of the two extraction methods is plotted (the classifier, by the text).
Place-cell code versus axis code

Two ways to code 256 positions in a vector space. Place code (O'Keefe's place cells): one direction per position, P≈I256​; all 256 directions have the same strength, so after centring the stable rank is 255 and the top-2 components explain only 2/255=0.8% of the variance (computed in check_04.py). Axis code (Chang and Tsao for faces): two directions, the row coordinate and the column coordinate; P has two columns that are ramps, stable rank 2, R2=1 (and the 256 positions form a flat sheet). The paper reads the evolution of Fig. 14 as a move from the first to the second.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: at 0 the position code is a place code: the sheet is a random cloud, stable rank is 255. Slide towards the axis code: two directions emerge, the cloud unfolds into the 16×16 sheet, the stable rank goes to 2 and R2 to 1. The mixture is a toy that we built; the real layers are in Figs. 14 and 15.

Inconsistency in Fig. 14 — layer axes, and a stable rank above 2 with R2≈1

(1) The two panels do not use the same layer axis: R2 is plotted for layers 0–11, stable rank for layers 1–12. (2) The values are incompatible for one centred matrix. Let R2=(σ12​+σ22​)/∑r​σr2​. Then srank=∑σr2​/σ12​=(σ12​+σ22​)/(R2σ12​)≤2/R2, because σ2​≤σ1​. At R2≈1 this gives srank≤2, while the last three layers read 2.8, 2.6, 2.7. For all 12 pairs of values the stable rank exceeds 2/R2 (check_04.py, figure below).

So the two panels are not computed on the same object: for instance the stable rank on the raw P and R2 on a centred (or otherwise processed) version, or a different definition of R2. The text does not say. The qualitative message (rank decreases with depth towards a sheet) is unaffected; a quantitative claim such as "stable rank converges to 2" is not what the plot shows (it stays at about 2.6–2.8).

Figure 15: PCA of the position basis across layers#

How to read this figure
  • Left. The colour of each grid cell (a smooth two-coordinate colour map), used to colour the dots.
  • Right. Layers 0,2,4,6,8: blobs of unordered colours (in layer 8 some bands appear); layers 9,10,11: the dots form a grid-like sheet where neighbouring colours are neighbours, a curved quadrilateral (the rows bend), with the left–right and top–bottom structure of the colour map.
  • Conclusion. Position is compressed to a 2-D sheet at the end ("coarse spatial priors").
  • Note. It is a sheet, not a flat plane: the rows bend. It is also consistent with the dense positional concepts of section 1.
  • Does not show. A numerical measure of the flatness of the sheet; for layers 1, 3, 5, 7 nothing is plotted.

Bottom of Fig. 14: where position sits in a per-image PCA#

How to read this figure
  • Left. The cumulative explained variance climbs fast: 15 components capture about 81% (read off a marked point). With 256 tokens in 768 dimensions, at most 255 components are non-trivial; 15 is 6% of that.
  • Right. The cosine of each per-image component with "Pos comp. 1" and "Pos comp. 2" (the top two directions of P). It peaks at component 5 for Pos comp. 1 (0.24) and component 3 for Pos comp. 2 (0.19), then falls to nearly 0.
  • Reading. Position is not in the dominant components (1, 2) of an image's token cloud but in the 3rd–5th. In R768 two random directions have ∣cos∣≈0.036, so 0.19–0.24 is about 5–7 times chance, but the angle is still about 76∘–79∘.
  • Not shown. Which layer (presumably the last) and over how many images ("on average").

Figure 27: smoothness survives position removal#

The test: project each token onto the orthogonal complement of the position subspace (the span of the classifier directions) and redo the PCA map.

How to read this figure
  • What is drawn. Same kind of map as Figs. 12–13, for one image, after removing the position subspace.
  • What to look at. Colour regions still follow the rabbit and its surroundings.
  • Authors' conclusion. Smoothness is "genuine semantic organization rather than artifacts of positional encoding".
  • Does not show. A quantitative comparison before and after; the layer used; more than one image (the main text points to this figure for the claim).
Our reading — removing a linear subspace is not removing position

The projection removes what a linear classifier uses at one layer. The positional information that is left (nonlinearly coded, or in directions the classifier does not use) is not removed. And the map would be smooth even without any position code, since neighbouring patches share content. The experiment excludes the explanation "smooth because of the 2-D position sheet", which is what it is designed for. See page 6.

Reflex

When you see "the rank collapses to 2" → ask on which matrix (centred or not, which layers, which extraction) and compare with the bound srank≤2/R2.

9. Toward interpolative geometry#

After excluding position as the only cause, the paper proposes that patch tokens are smooth mixtures of a discrete set of "landmark" prototypes, and finds support in the DINOv2 training heads. This is a conjecture; it is the bridge to the Minkowski hypothesis of page 5.

Toward interpolative geometry §6 · p. 16

"[...] across many images, patch tokens occupy a consistent low dimensional and locally connected set that aligns with object and coherent regions. First, this stability across images suggest that embeddings are not purely relative. Second, [...] the connectedness is not explained by position alone [...]. What remains is the possibility that tokens interpolate smoothly between a discrete set of anchor points or landmark representations. This interpolative structure finds natural support in DINOv2's training objectives. The global DINO head matches teacher representations using 128k prototypes, while the iBOT head performs masked prediction with its own 128k prototype vocabulary. The Kozachenko–Leonenko regularizer further encourages entropy maximization, promoting uniform distribution across the representation space while avoiding collapse. Rather than learning arbitrary smooth manifolds, this setup naturally favors representations that can be expressed as mixtures of multiple prototype sets. [...] This suggests that the observed connectedness may arise not from continuous interpolation per se, but from discrete mixing of archetypal points."

What each ingredient is#

DINO head
maps the image-level feature to scores over 128k prototypes; teacher and student probability vectors (softmax over prototypes) are matched by a cross-entropy. more
iBOT head
the same idea for masked patch tokens, with its own 128k prototypes. more
footnote of the paper
each head is an MLP 4096→4096→256 producing scores over 128k prototypes, followed by softmax, "effectively implementing implicit clustering with soft assignments" (stated by the paper; we did not check it against the DINOv2 code).
KoLeo (Kozachenko–Leonenko)
a regulariser that spreads the features in a batch by penalising small nearest-neighbour distances, i.e. a nearest-neighbour entropy estimate. more
"mixtures of prototypes"
a softmax output p∈ΔK is a point of a simplex: a weighted combination of the prototypes with weights summing to 1. This is exactly the form of an archetypal (convex) code, which is why the paper links it to what comes next.

Claimed, and conjectured#

StatementStatus
Patch tokens of different images share a low-dimensional frame; maps are smooth (Figs. 12, 13, 22)suggestive: qualitative, few images
Position alone does not explain it (Figs. 14, 27)suggestive: linear subspace only
DINO and iBOT heads have 128k prototypes with softmax assignmentsstated by the paper (architecture)
KoLeo spreads features uniformly, avoiding collapseits purpose, as stated in the DINOv2 method
"This setup naturally favours" tokens as mixtures of landmarks of several prototype setsspeculative: no derivation, no measurement
Connectedness comes from "discrete mixing of archetypal points" rather than continuous interpolationspeculative
Our reading — three gaps between the heads and the backbone tokens
  • The prototypes live in the space of the head's output (after the MLP and a normalisation), not in the 768-dimensional token space that Fig. 12 shows. A mixture of prototypes there says nothing yet about a convex combination of tokens in R768.
  • Softmax weights over 128k prototypes with a low temperature are nearly one-hot; the claim of rich mixtures would need the weights to be spread, which the paper does not measure.
  • The paper does not say on which tokens KoLeo acts; if it acts only on image-level features, it says nothing about patch tokens (page 1 recalls the definition).

This is the weak link between §6 and the MRH of page 5; page 5 then argues from the attention mechanism instead. See page 6.

10. Summary and reflexes#

What to remember
  • Occurrence (Fig. 9 A–C). Conditional energy against firing count has a triangular envelope; three dense positional concepts (left, right, bottom) fire on about 26–31% of tokens (our estimate) and take about 11% of all activations: a hybrid sparse + dense code.
  • Co-activation (Fig. 9 right). The spectrum of Z⊤Z is smooth, between a random and a shuffled baseline that differ by a factor of about 1.3: weak evidence of no modules.
  • Geometry (Fig. 10). Welch 0.0356; Grassmannian 0.0659; random up to about 0.23; the SAE up to about 0.9. Singular values: tight-frame level 6.455, MP band [5.45,7.45], SAE from 22.5 down to 0: anisotropy. Hoyer 0.22–0.25: distributed atoms.
  • Antipodal pairs (Fig. 11 A). A signed feature needs two opposite atoms when codes are non-negative; beware of cosine similarity.
  • Usage versus geometry (Fig. 11 B). r=0.28, R2=0.08; tr[Z⊤ZDD⊤]=∥ZD∥F2​≥0 explains why some positive relation is unavoidable, but not the Pearson coefficient.
  • PCA maps (Figs. 12, 13, 22). A linear map takes a segment to a segment or a point, so it adds no curvature; it can still hide differences. A shared basis aligns five snow leopards.
  • Position (Figs. 14, 15, 27). Decoding ≈1.0→0.23 over layers; stable rank 9.0→2.7; R2 of top-2 0.63→1.0 (inconsistent with the stable rank); 15 per-image components hold 81%; position sits in components 3 and 5; smoothness survives position removal.
  • Interpolative geometry. A conjecture based on prototype heads and KoLeo; the bridge to page 5.

Reflexes#

  • A dictionary spectrum → compare with c/d​ and the Marchenko–Pastur band, not with a flat line at 1.
  • A "coherence" claim → compare with the Welch bound (0.0356) and with the best known frame (0.0659), not with 0.
  • Two opposite atoms → a signed feature under non-negative codes; use ∣cos∣ if the sign is not the point.
  • A correlation between Z⊤Z and DD⊤ → ask whether the diagonal is in; the trace identity makes a positive uncentred inner product automatic.
  • A smooth PCA map → it shows the top-3 coordinates are smooth, and that projection cannot add curvature; it does not show connectedness in R768.
  • "Rank collapses to 2" → on which matrix? Check srank≤2/R2.
  • "Mixtures of prototypes" → in which space, with what weights?

What the next page does with it#

The observations of this page (dense positional concepts, anisotropy, antipodal pairs, locally connected token clouds, tokens as mixtures) are the motivation of page 5: the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis replaces the cone of the LRH by sums of polytopes built from archetypes, and derives it from the structure of attention. How far these observations support it is discussed on page 6.

Exercises#

Graded from ★ (direct use) to ★★★ (needs an argument). Numbers can be recomputed with checks/check_04.py.

Exercise 1 — Slots taken by dense concepts ★

Two concepts fire on 29% of the tokens each, and k=8. (a) How many of the 8 slots do they take per token on average? (b) What share of all activations? (c) How does it change if k=32?

Hint

The expected number of active entries among the two is 2×0.29. A token has k slots on average.

Solution

(a) 2×0.29=0.58 slots per token. (b) 0.58/8=7.25%. (c) 0.58/32=1.8%: the same dense concepts weigh four times less when the code has four times more slots. This does not use independence: expectations add.

Exercise 2 — Reference values of a dictionary ★

For c=10,000 unit atoms in d=100: give the Welch bound, the tight-frame singular value, and the Marchenko–Pastur band for random atoms.

Hint

(c−d)/(d(c−1))​; c/d​; c/d​(1±d/c​).

Solution

Welch: 9900/(100×9999)​=0.0995. Tight frame: 100​=10. d/c​=0.1, band =10×[0.9,1.1]=[9,11]. Check: ∑σ2=100×100=10,000=c.

Exercise 3 — A signed feature with non-negative codes ★★

The activation is a=xu and the dictionary has atoms u, −u and a third atom w with ⟨u,w⟩=0. (a) Give the code for x=−2. (b) Give cos and ∣cos∣ for the antipodal pair, and the coherence of the three atoms. (c) A clustering by cosine puts the pair in the same cluster or in different clusters?

Hint

Write xu=z1​u+z2​(−u) with z1​,z2​≥0.

Solution

(a) z=(0,2,0), because 2⋅(−u)=−2u. (b) cos=−1, ∣cos∣=1, coherence μ=max∣⟨⋅,⋅⟩∣=1 (the pair), although the three atoms represent only two directions. (c) A cosine-distance clustering sees cos=−1 as maximal distance: different clusters. Using ∣cos∣ would merge them. Which is right depends on whether the sign carries meaning.

Exercise 4 — The trace identity on a small example ★★

Z=​101​011​​, D=(10.6​00.8​). Compute G=Z⊤Z, K=DD⊤, tr[GK] and ∥ZD∥F2​.

Hint

tr[GK]=∑ij​Gij​Kij​ for symmetric matrices.

Solution

G=(21​12​), K=(10.6​0.61​). tr[GK]=2+0.6+0.6+2=5.2. ZD has rows (1,0), (0.6,0.8), (1.6,0.8) with squared norms 1, 1, 3.2: sum 5.2. They agree. Note that the two diagonal terms give 4 of the 5.2: the diagonal dominates.

Exercise 5 — Stable rank against R2 ★★

Show srank(P)≤2/R2 where R2 is the share of the squared Frobenius norm held by the top two singular values. Apply it to the last layer of Fig. 14 (R2≈1.00, stable rank 2.7) and say what follows.

Hint

Write ∑σr2​=(σ12​+σ22​)/R2 and use σ2​≤σ1​.

Solution

srank=∑σr2​/σ12​=(σ12​+σ22​)/(R2σ12​)≤2σ12​/(R2σ12​)=2/R2. For R2=1 the bound is 2, so 2.7 is impossible on one matrix; even for R2=0.99 it is 2.02. The two panels are not computed on the same object (e.g. raw versus centred); the paper does not say.

Exercise 6 — Place code and axis code ★★

(a) The place code of a 16×16 grid is P=I256​. Compute the stable rank and the R2 of the top two components of the centred matrix. (b) The axis code has two columns, the row index and the column index (centred and scaled to equal norm). Same questions. (c) Which is closer to layer 0 and which to layer 11 of Fig. 14?

Hint

Centring I256​ removes one direction (the all-ones vector). All remaining singular values of the centred identity equal 1.

Solution

(a) 255 equal singular values: stable rank 255; R2=2/255=0.8%. (b) Two equal singular values: stable rank 2, R2=1 (the two ramps are orthogonal after centring, since rows and columns are independent coordinates). (c) Layer 0 is far from the place code too (R2=0.63, stable rank 9): even the first layer already has a few dominant directions; layer 11 is close to the axis code. The paper's place-cell wording is an analogy, not a measured match.

Exercise 7 — What a smooth PCA map implies ★★★

(a) Prove that a projection P with orthonormal rows satisfies ∥Px−Py∥≤∥x−y∥. (b) Give two tokens with identical colour in a PCA map that are far apart in R768. (c) What does a smooth map then prove about the tokens?

Hint

For (a): P⊤P is an orthogonal projector. For (b): move along a direction orthogonal to the three components.

Solution

(a) ∥Pv∥2=v⊤P⊤Pv=​P⊤Pv​2+…; more simply P⊤P is the orthogonal projector onto the row space, and a projector does not increase the norm: ∥Pv∥=​P⊤Pv​≤∥v∥ with v=x−y. (b) y=x+10e with e a unit vector orthogonal to the three principal directions: same three coordinates, distance 10. (c) Only that the three coordinates vary slowly: closeness in R768 implies closeness in colour, not conversely. Connectedness in R768 needs a separate argument.

Exercise 8 — How spread is an atom with Hoyer 0.2? ★★★

An atom has k equal non-zero entries and 768−k zeros. For which k is its Hoyer score 0.2 (about the Gaussian value) and 0.25? Is an atom with score 0.25 "sparse"?

Hint

For k equal entries, ∥x∥1​/∥x∥2​=k​, so H=(n​−k​)/(n​−1). Solve for k.

Solution

k​=n​−H(n​−1), with 768​=27.71: H=0.2 gives k​=22.37, k≈500; H=0.25 gives k≈442. So a score of 0.25 corresponds to an atom with about 442 of its 768 coordinates equally active: very spread. "Slightly sparser than Gaussian" means "slightly less spread", and the atoms are far from neuron-aligned (k=1).
